title: So one programmer hid his name inside the game itself.
description:
So one programmer hid his name inside the game itself. Warren Robinett built Adventure for the Atari 2600, and slipped in a secret room Atari never approved.

You had to carry an almost-invisible object across the map to unlock it. Asked why, in his own words: "I was pissed."

A fifteen-year-old player who found the hidden room and mailed Atari a handwritten letter describing it, the first record of anyone outside Atari finding Robinett's secret.

An employee named Steve Wright coined the term "Easter egg". His reasoning: hiding things in games was a good thing, "like Easter eggs for players to find". The name stuck across the whole industry.

The first hidden secret in console gaming was a protest note.

Sources:
- https://atari.com/blogs/atari/so-let-s-talk-about-that-easter-egg: Atari's own company blog ("Game History", 5 Jul 2022), read in full. Establishes: Atari's policy at the time was not to publicly credit individual developers; Warren Robinett, designing Adventure for the Atari 2600 (development underway through 1979), hid a secret room displaying his own signature; in his own words, "I was pissed"; the term "Easter Egg" did not exist yet; fifteen-year-old Adam Clayton discovered the room and told Atari in a handwritten letter; an Atari employee, Steve Wright, is believed to have coined "Easter Egg" afterward, framing hidden surprises as good, "like Easter eggs for players to find"; the practice spread across the industry from there.
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adventure_(1980_video_game): via search summary, corroborating: Robinett designed and coded Adventure alone for the Atari 2600, and it is credited as the first widely publicised Easter egg in a console video game.
